questions.question_text: Determine whether $f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x - 1, & x \le 2 \\ x^{2} + 1, & x > 2 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x = 2$.

options.text: Discontinuous at $x = 2$, because the subfunctions are defined by different algebraic formulas.
options.why: Assumed having different formulas automatically creates a discontinuity regardless of values.

options.text: Discontinuous at $x = 2$, because the left branch evaluates to $4$ and the right branch to $5$.
options.why: Made an arithmetic error evaluating $3(2) - 1$ as $4$ instead of $5$.

options.text: Discontinuous at $x = 2$, because $x > 2$ is a strict inequality.
options.why: Confused a strict domain inequality with a graph discontinuity.

questions.solution_text:
Evaluate both subfunctions at $x = 2$:
Left branch: $3(2) - 1 = 5$
Right branch: $(2)^{2} + 1 = 5$
Since both branches agree at $y = 5$, $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = 2$.

options.why: Stated the $y$-value of the filled dot instead of the $x$-value of the discontinuity.
Pointed to the $y$-intercept rather than the point of discontinuity.
Pointed to the left boundary of the plotted window instead of the discontinuity.

At $x = 2$, the line approaches $y = 2$ from both sides, but $g(2) = 4$.
The function is discontinuous at $x = 2$.

questions.question_text: Determine whether $f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 1, & x \le 3 \\ x^{2} - 2, & x > 3 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x = 3$.

options.text: Continuous, because both branches approach $7$ and $f(3) = 7$.
Discontinuous, because the left branch approaches $6$ and the right branch approaches $7$.
options.why: Omitted the $+1$ when evaluating $2(3) + 1$.

options.text: Discontinuous, because the left branch approaches $7$ and the right branch approaches $11$.

options.why: Ignored that the condition $x \le 3$ includes the boundary.

questions.solution_text:
Evaluate both subfunctions at $x = 3$:
Left branch: $2(3) + 1 = 7$
Right branch: $3^{2} - 2 = 7$
The defined value is $f(3) = 7$, so the function is continuous at $x = 3$.

questions.question_text: At which values of $x$ is the rational function $f(x) = \dfrac{5}{x^{2} - 5x}$ discontinuous?

options.why: Divided by $x$ and forgot that $x = 0$ makes the denominator zero.
Found $x = 0$ but omitted the second root $x = 5$ of $x(x - 5) = 0$.
Confused $x^{2} - 5x$ with the difference of squares $x^{2} - 25$.

questions.solution_text:
Set the denominator equal to zero:
$x^{2} - 5x = 0$
$x(x - 5) = 0$
$x = 0$ or $x = 5$

questions.question_text: Determine all values of $x$ where $f(x) = \dfrac{x^{2} - 9}{x^{2} - 4}$ is discontinuous.

options.why: Set the numerator equal to zero instead of the denominator.
Omitted the negative root when solving $x^{2} = 4$.
Combined the zeroes of both the numerator and the denominator.

questions.solution_text:
Discontinuities occur where the denominator is zero:
$x^{2} - 4 = 0$
$(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0$
$x = -2, 2$

questions.question_text: Determine whether $f(x) = \begin{cases} 4 - x, & x < 1 \\ x^{2} + 4, & x \ge 1 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x = 1$.

options.text: Discontinuous, because the left branch approaches $3$ and the right branch approaches $5$.

options.why: Assumed a defined boundary value guarantees continuity without comparing the neighbouring branches.
Evaluated $4 - 1$ as $5$ by adding instead of subtracting.
Ignored that the condition $x \ge 1$ defines $f(1)$.

questions.solution_text:
Evaluate left and right branches at $x = 1$:
Left branch: $4 - 1 = 3$
Right branch and defined value: $1^{2} + 4 = 5$
Since $3 \neq 5$, the function is discontinuous at $x = 1$.

questions.question_text: State all values of $x$ at which a discontinuity occurs for $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^{2} - 5, & x < -3 \\ 4, & x = -3 \\ 1 - x, & -3 < x < 2 \\ 0, & x = 2 \\ x^{2} - 5, & x > 2 \end{cases}$.

options.why: Treated a separately defined point as automatically discontinuous at $x = -3$, and overlooked the incorrect height at $x = 2$.
Assumed both boundaries are discontinuities without checking that all three values at $x = -3$ equal $4$.
Compared only the neighbouring branches and ignored that $f(2) = 0$ differs from their common approached value $-1$.

questions.solution_text:
At $x = -3$:
Left branch: $(-3)^{2} - 5 = 4$
Defined value: $f(-3) = 4$
Right branch: $1 - (-3) = 4$
The function is continuous at $x = -3$.
At $x = 2$:
Left branch: $1 - 2 = -1$
Right branch: $2^{2} - 5 = -1$
However, $f(2) = 0$, so the function is discontinuous at $x = 2$.
The only discontinuity is at $x = 2$.

questions.question_text: State all values of $x$ at which a discontinuity occurs for $f(x)=\begin{cases}3&x\le-2\\-x+1&-2<x<4\\-2&x\ge4\end{cases}$.

options.why: Evaluated $-(-2)+1$ as $-1$ instead of $3$, and overlooked the unequal values at $x = 4$.
Assumed every change of formula creates a discontinuity, although the branches agree at $x = -2$.
Checked only the matching values at $x = -2$ and omitted the comparison at $x = 4$.

questions.solution_text:
At $x = -2$, the left branch and defined value are $3$, and the middle branch approaches $-(-2)+1=3$, so the function is continuous.
At $x = 4$, the middle branch approaches $-4+1=-3$, while the right branch and defined value are $-2$. These differ, so the function is discontinuous at $x = 4$ only.

questions.question_text: Consider the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2&-1\le x<0\\2x&0\le x<1\\1&x=1\\-2x+4&1<x<2\\0&2<x<3.\end{cases}$ Its domain is $D=[-1,2)\cup(2,3)$. For what values of $x$ in $D$ is $f(x)$ continuous?

options.why: Assumed the change of formula at $x = 0$ creates a discontinuity, although both branches approach the defined value $0$.
Treated the included domain endpoint $x = -1$ as discontinuous, although the graph approaches $f(-1)=1$ from within its domain.
Ignored that the neighbouring branches approach $2$ at $x = 1$, while $f(1)=1$.

questions.solution_text: At $x=0$, both neighbouring branches approach $0$ and $f(0)=0$, so the function is continuous. At $x=1$, both neighbouring branches approach $2$ but $f(1)=1$, so it is discontinuous. The value $x=2$ is undefined and is excluded from $D$; it is not a defined point to test. At the included endpoint $x=-1$, the graph approaches $f(-1)=1$ from within its domain. Hence the function is continuous at every value in $D$ except $x=1$.
